decisions.claim: Set-ExplicitAcl does not build an allowlist: /inheritance:r removes only INHERITED aces, and /grant adds without removing, so an explicit Users grant survives a reinstall
decisions.reason: Confirmed on win199 by planting icacls /grant Users:(OI)(CI)(RX) and re-running the installer -- before the fix the grant survived and the installer printed 'the boundary' over it. Now /reset (drops every explicit ace, restores inheritance) then /inheritance:r (empty DACL) then the grants, so the grants are the entire contents. Re-tested on the box: the planted grant is gone, the ACL is exactly the three allowed SIDs, protected=True, owner=Administrators.

decisions.claim: the reparse-point defence is check-then-use and does not validate the Base/State/Run path components
decisions.reason: Both halves true. Now checks EVERY component of each path, not just the leaf, and creates store.key with FileMode.CreateNew so an existing entry -- including a link planted after the check -- fails the write instead of being followed. Still not atomic, and the code says so: PowerShell cannot open a path with FILE_FLAG_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT, so there is no atomic form available here. What bounds it is that only the service account can write in that directory, so the attacker must already BE a compromised broker, which is out of scope for every phase so far and is what phase 9's signed binary addresses.

decisions.claim: the installer prints the task state but never treats a stopped or failed task as an installation failure
decisions.reason: Confirmed. It now waits, then requires State=Running AND at least one node process owned by the service account, and Fails with the three usual causes named. The reviewer's repro (a wrong -NodePath) would previously have reached 'Done' and exited 0.

decisions.claim: RightWith tests for an existing SID by substring, so ...-1001 matches inside ...-10010
decisions.reason: Confirmed, and the consequence is the worst available: it concludes the right is already granted, omits our SID, and the task then silently never runs -- the exact failure the function exists to prevent. Now splits on commas and compares whole tokens. The same bug was in two places in the verifier; both fixed.

decisions.claim: the verifier's TCP handshake has no deadline, so a required check can hang instead of failing
decisions.reason: Confirmed. BeginConnect with a 5s wait, ReceiveTimeout/SendTimeout/ReadTimeout at 10s. A check that hangs never reaches the exit code, which is worse than one that fails.

decisions.claim: the verifier reports the banner 'signed' after checking only that sig is a string longer than 40 characters
decisions.reason: Confirmed -- a check that could not fail, which is the shape I care most about. PowerShell 5.1 runs on .NET Framework, which has no ImportSubjectPublicKeyInfo, so verifying P-256 there is not available. Instead it now asks TWICE with different nonces and requires different signatures plus a plausible DER length: a broker signs the nonce it was given, a replayed banner cannot. Renamed to what it proves -- 'signs the nonce it was given, not a replay'. Full signature verification stays in the unit tests, against the key.

decisions.claim: the verifier takes over and then deletes any pre-existing account or task using its fixed probe names
decisions.reason: Confirmed and indefensible -- a verification script must not destroy things it did not create. The probe name is now random per run (wv-vfy-<8 hex>), and it refuses rather than adopts if that name somehow exists.

decisions.claim: a per-agent discovery publication failure leaves a partially serving daemon instead of refusing startup
decisions.reason: The behaviour is real and is deliberate, not an oversight. Spec check 8 is about not falling back to another port, which it does not. Killing the whole broker because one agent's discovery file could not be written takes every OTHER agent down with it, which is a worse outcome than one agent being unreachable and saying so. The reviewer had not been shown listenOn and flagged this as conditional, correctly. What IS weak is that the failure is one line on stderr; noted as an open item for a degraded-state field in ping rather than fixed here.

decisions.claim: machineIdentityFromSources does not implement the spec's derivation string
decisions.reason: The mismatch is real and the SPEC was the wrong half. The code labels each source (wv-win:smbios=...:machineguid=...); the spec wrote the unlabelled form. Labelled is correct: unlabelled, a machine with only an SMBIOS UUID and a machine with only a MachineGuid of the same value hash the same input. Spec amended, with the reason.

decisions.claim: consoleSafe is punctuation transliteration, not the specified guarantee of no non-ASCII output
decisions.reason: Confirmed -- an agent named Jose with an accent goes straight to the console. The promise is 'no non-ASCII reaches the Windows console', and our own prose is not the only thing printed: agent names, paths and upstream errors flow through the same writes. Anything left after transliteration is now escaped as \uXXXX, which keeps the name identifiable rather than mangling it to '?'. Acceptance check 28 widened.

decisions.claim: the boundary warning says the daemon runs as the agents' user even when a weakened ACL is the actual problem
decisions.reason: Confirmed, and exactly the discipline this codebase is built on -- a warning must not be the wrong warning. Two different failures were sharing one sentence. An installed daemon whose ACL was widened is still its own account; it now gets its own message saying the directory is open and the separation is not doing anything.

decisions.claim: blind spot: the combined machine identity is unstable if one source is transiently unavailable
decisions.reason: Real. A PowerShell hiccup drops the SMBIOS source, the identity changes, and the store will not decrypt. It fails SAFE -- the daemon refuses to serve or overwrite and says the store is unreadable -- so it is confusing rather than destructive, and the supported install path uses store.key rather than a derived key at all. Recorded as an open item: the fix is to record which sources produced the identity and refuse with an accurate message when the set changes, rather than silently deriving a different key.

decisions.claim: blind spot: the installer resets an existing account password before the ACL and task work is known to succeed
decisions.reason: True and low: a failure leaves an account whose password nobody knows, which the next run of the installer fixes, because that is the first thing it does. Noted.

decisions.claim: blind spot: SeDenyBatchLogonRight inherited through group membership or a later GPO is not detected
decisions.reason: Real but niche. Its effect is caught downstream -- the installer now FAILS when the task registers and the broker is not running (F3), which is what a denied logon right produces. Noted rather than checked directly.

decisions.claim: blind spot: NodePath and AgentPath are checked for existence, not for whether ordinary users can rewrite them
decisions.reason: Promoted, because it is the boundary's whole point: the task runs that file as an account holding every credential on the machine, so whoever can replace it chooses what the broker executes and the separation starts protecting their code. nvm-windows installs node under %APPDATA%, which is exactly that. The installer warns loudly (refusing would lock out every nvm user) and the VERIFIER fails on it, so 'verified' still means verified. It fired truthfully on win199 first time -- C:\nodejs was writable by Users -- and the box was locked down rather than the check softened.

decisions.claim: blind spot: the verifier adds the probe SID to SeBatchLogonRight and never removes it
decisions.reason: Confirmed: deleting the account leaves its raw SID in local security policy, so every run left another dead entry in a list nobody reads. The finally block now removes it.

decisions.claim: blind spot: the second-broker check is a preflight race, not a lock
decisions.reason: Correct, and already documented as exactly that in the code. Two daemons starting in the same millisecond could both find nothing. It closes the case that actually happens -- a second start while the first is running, which occurred during this phase's own testing -- and claims nothing more.
